summary: This informational document examines problems that arise when providers share one IPv4 address among many subscribers due to address exhaustion. It looks at several emerging solutions and their effects on applications. It is analysis, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: When several subscribers use one public IPv4 address, the address alone no longer identifies one subscriber or device. This memo explains effects on applications, service providers, content services, and traceability.

subtitle: The operational and application problems that arise when subscribers share public IPv4 addresses.

tldr.problem: Providers face a shortage of public IPv4 addresses and are considering ways to share addresses among subscribers.
tldr.mechanism: The memo surveys problems common to shared-address designs, including port allocation, application compatibility, location, logging, security, and network operations.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that IPv6 deployment is the only perennial way to ease pressure on the public IPv4 pool without address-sharing mechanisms and their associated issues.

today: RFC 6269 is an Informational memo published in June 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document analyzes shared-address issues rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Why Providers Share Addresses
sections.content:
IANA completed its IPv4 address allocations on February 3, 2011. The memo describes service providers' concern that they may not have enough public addresses to assign one to each subscriber. It surveys issues common to shared-address approaches rather than choosing or specifying one solution.

It says deploying IPv6 is the only perennial way to ease pressure on the public IPv4 pool without address-sharing mechanisms. In the shorter term, sharing may support continued IPv4 service, but the resulting problems can affect end users, providers, content providers, and law-enforcement agencies.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers may let multiple subscribers use one public IPv4 address because the supply is limited. That makes it harder for services to distinguish subscribers and can affect how applications work.

sections.title: Two Broad Sharing Approaches
sections.content:
The memo describes two broad classes. A provider-operated Carrier Grade NAT (CGN) translates subscribers' private addresses to a smaller pool of public addresses. Named examples include NAT444 and Dual-Stack Lite. A port-range design gives several subscribers the same public address but assigns each a different, non-overlapping port range.

These approaches differ in how translation and ports are managed, but the memo focuses on their shared external effects. It notes that traditional home NAT generally concerns one legal entity, while large-scale sharing can involve several subscribers and organizations at once.
sections.plainLanguage: One approach translates traffic through a provider's shared NAT. Another assigns each subscriber a separate range of ports on the shared address. Both can make one address serve multiple subscribers.

sections.title: Port Allocation and Incoming Connections
sections.content:
For outgoing connections, the source port is often less important to the application, although port-range designs restrict which source ports a subscriber may use. For incoming connections, the port matters because outside services use it to reach a subscriber's service. TCP ports in TIME-WAIT, typically for 4 minutes after a connection ends, still count when estimating port demand.

Dynamic allocation from a shared pool can accommodate uneven demand better than fixed per-subscriber allocations, but it increases the provider's logging burden. A subscriber using many connections can also consume shared resources, so the memo says limits may be needed. Incoming port forwarding requires cooperation between customer equipment and a provider CGN; fixed well-known ports and UDP service discovery may not work generally under sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: Outgoing and incoming connections use ports differently. Sharing can restrict which ports a subscriber uses and can make it harder for outside systems to start a connection to a service at home.

sections.title: Application and Network Effects
sections.content:
Applications may fail if they need inbound connections, embed addresses or ports in message data, rely on fixed ports, treat an IP address as a unique device identifier, or prohibit simultaneous users from one address. The proposals discussed in the memo support TCP, UDP, and ICMP; other protocols named in the text include SCTP, DCCP, RSVP, IPv6-over-IPv4, and IPsec ESP.

ICMP has no port field, so address-sharing systems need special handling to route some messages. Fragmented packets also need special handling because only the first fragment carries TCP or UDP port information. The memo discusses further effects on path MTU discovery, geo-location and proximity, usage monitoring, reverse DNS, load balancing, IPv6 transition mechanisms, single points of failure, multicast, Mobile IP, and battery use from frequent keep-alives.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs that assume an IP address identifies one device may confuse multiple subscribers who share that address. Some protocols and message types also lack the port information a sharing system needs to direct traffic.

sections.title: Traceability, Abuse Handling, and Security
sections.content:
A shared public address no longer identifies one subscriber by itself. The memo describes logging the source port at servers along with the source address and timestamp, or logging destination addresses at the provider. It considers destination logging less reliable when several subscribers contact the same server. Providers may need to retain address mappings for periods determined by local jurisdiction.

Address-based penalty boxes, spam blacklists, and access controls can affect all subscribers sharing an address, including people who did nothing wrong. Smaller port pools can also make port randomization harder. The memo says shared-address systems should be assessed for security effects and should apply ingress filtering so outgoing source addresses or ports are set correctly. It defines no protocol and says it creates no new security issues of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: To identify one subscriber, a service may need the address, port, and time, while a provider must keep matching records. Blocking one shared address can also block innocent subscribers who use it.
